As demand for artificial intelligence continues to reshape the global data landscape, investors are weighing the explosive growth of Credo Technology Group (NASDAQ:CRDO) against the established dominance of Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL).

Credo specializes in energy-efficient connectivity for high-speed networks, focusing on specific bottlenecks in hyperscale data centers. Marvell offers a more diverse range of semiconductor solutions covering storage, optical, and computing needs across the entire networking ecosystem. Comparing these two reveals a choice between a high-growth specialist and a diversified infrastructure giant.

The case for Credo Technology Group

Credo focuses on designing high-speed copper and optical interconnect solutions that facilitate massive data movements within cloud networks. The company primarily serves blue chip hyperscalers and equipment manufacturers, with high-profile partnerships including Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT). Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as nearly 90% of revenue in its latest annual report came from just 10 customers.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached close to $1.6 billion, representing explosive growth of approximately 165.1% compared to the prior period. This rapid scaling helped the company generate a net income of roughly $538.3 million during that time frame. The resulting net margin of 33.8% highlights how effectively the company is translating its semiconductor stock sales into actual earnings as it expands.

As of its May 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio, which measures whether a company can cover its short-term debts with short-term assets, is 10.2x. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x, indicating a balance sheet with no total debt relative to shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended May 2, 2026, free cash flow was approximately $407.0 million. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 39.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow in the cash flow statement.

The case for Marvell Technology

Marvell Technology provides the foundational hardware required to move, store, and process data across cloud and automotive markets. The company has a strong focus on the data center segment, which is increasingly driven by demand for custom silicon and high-speed networking. Marvell also maintains high customer concentration, as its top 10 customers accounted for roughly 82% of its revenue in its latest annual report.

title: Billionaire Bill Ackman Says There’s a Huge Disconnect in Wall Street’s Expectations for Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Alphabet
detail:
Billionaire Bill Ackman Says There’s a Huge Disconnect in Wall Street’s Expectations for Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Alphabet
Adam Levy, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 7:05 AM PST 5 min read
GOOGN
AMZN
MSFT
META
^GSPC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The stock market hasn't been as keen on the hyperscalers in 2026 as it was in years past. Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) have delivered better returns than the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) year to date thanks to strong relative performances over the past month or so. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) haven't fared nearly as well — they're down for the year.

But that could be an opportunity for long-term retail investors. Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman believes the market has soured on these four stocks due to a "notable disconnect" between market expectations and the businesses' fundamentals. That's reflected in growing skepticism among analysts that the massive amounts these companies are spending on new data centers will yield meaningful returns on investment.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

But the actual financial results and management's commentary should give investors confidence that the future may be brighter for these hyperscalers than the average analyst expects.

Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman. Image source: Getty Images.

The huge disconnect on Wall Street

In his third-quarter letter to Pershing Square shareholders, Ackman expressed his belief that most analysts aren't properly accounting for the potential revenue growth stemming from the stepped-up capital spending among Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Alphabet. He wrote:

Consensus analyst estimates for the hyperscalers reflect a notable disconnect: they expect the current level of capital intensity to persist for years into the future, yet they assume minimal acceleration in revenue growth beyond this year and next. Consensus estimates treat the capex buildout as a structural increase in maintenance capital intensity rather than as an investment capable of producing outsized future revenue growth and attractive returns on capital.

That is to say, Wall Street is acting like the increase in capital expenditures won't result in a commensurate increase in revenue over time. That's despite the fact that their prior spending has already been doing so for all four hyperscalers.

Meta, notably, saw accelerating growth in its advertising business as it accelerated its capital expenditures. And with the potential to grow its Muse agentic AI service, expand business messaging, and collect licensing revenue from its large language models (LLMs), it could see a sharp rise in direct artificial intelligence monetization in the near future.

title: C3.ai vs. SentinelOne: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

C3.ai vs. SentinelOne: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

S

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping how corporations operate, but choosing between C3.ai (NYSE:AI) and SentinelOne (NYSE:S) requires understanding two very different approaches to software deployment.

C3.ai focuses on prebuilt applications that help large organizations optimize complex workflows. SentinelOne operates in the critical cybersecurity niche, using automated intelligence to protect endpoints and cloud data from sophisticated digital threats.

The case for C3.ai

C3.ai sells a specialized platform that enables businesses to deploy agentic AI applications tailored to specific industries. The company relies on deep strategic relationships with Baker Hughes (NASDAQ:BKR) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) to reach large industrial and cloud customers.

In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue reached approximately $232.4 million, a decrease of nearly 37.5% from the prior year. During the same period, the company reported a net loss of nearly $446.4 million as it continues to navigate a transition in its sales model.

As of its April 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x, and the current ratio is roughly 6.6x. The current ratio measures a company's ability to pay short-term obligations with its short-term assets. In the fiscal year ended April 30, 2026, free cash flow was negative $190.7 million, representing the cash remaining after operating costs and capital investments.

The case for SentinelOne

SentinelOne provides the Singularity Platform, an autonomous security solution that protects organizations from cyberattacks. The company is a prominent player among tech stocks, using partnerships with N-able (NYSE:NABL), Cloudflare (NYSE:NET), and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) to scale its distribution globally.

In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue was approximately $1.1 billion, representing growth of approximately 21.1% over the preceding 12 months. Despite this top-line expansion, the company recorded a net loss of nearly $340.1 million during that time frame.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is close to 1.4x, and the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was approximately $75.9 million. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 388.4% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back.

Risk profile comparison

C3.ai faces financial instability due to a history of net losses and an accumulated deficit that reached nearly $1.8 billion by early 2026. The business relies heavily on a limited number of high-value customer contracts, and it continues to face intense competition from established cloud providers and internal IT organizations.

title: Nvidia, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Micron Are All Buying Anthropic’s IPO. Should You Buy Too?
detail:
Nvidia, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Micron Are All Buying Anthropic’s IPO. Should You Buy Too?
Adam Levy, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 2:22 AM PST 5 min read
ANTH.PVT
GOOGN
NVDA
MSFT
MU
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Anthropic is set to be one of the biggest IPOs in history. The frontier AI lab revealed plans to sell 825 million shares of Class A stock at a share price between $70 and $78. At the high end of that range, it'll raise $64 billion and imply a fully diluted valuation of $1.4 trillion.

Separately, Anthropic is raising $26 billion in a private placement of the company's Class N shares, which carry no voting rights (but convert to Class A shares if sold to an unaffiliated buyer). That share class allows strategic business partners, including Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Micron Techology (NASDAQ:MU), and others, to invest in the company without conflict of interest. Indeed, all four companies are on the roster of investors in the private placement, buying shares at the same price as the IPO.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The question investors need to ask is: Are the big tech companies getting yet another deal on Anthropic shares? And if so, should you join them now that average investors finally have an opportunity to buy the stock?

Image source: Getty Images.

What happened to the $2 trillion IPO?

Just a few weeks ago, many analysts speculated that Anthropic could make its public debut with a $2 trillion valuation. That'd be a huge jump from the $965 billion valuation it garnered in its last fundraising round in May. Even so, the bottom of the company's IPO range represents an increase of about 30% in value in less than six months.

Anthropic is going public just as investors are expressing heightened concerns about artificial intelligence stocks. There's growing skepticism that the huge amounts being spent on new data centers will produce a meaningful return on investment. What's more, the midterm elections clearly show the public's opposition to building more data centers, with new officials who could slow the development of the so-called "AI factories."

Meanwhile, Anthropic disclosed commitments of nearly $900 billion in spending, about half of which will occur before the end of 2030. As such, the continued build-out of data centers is integral to Anthropic's growth. So, the current environment has weighed on its value.

Nonetheless, Anthropic is moving forward with its IPO despite the market pullback in AI investments. That's in contrast to rival OpenAI, which has delayed its public debut until at least next year.

CoreWeave Jumped 20% and Pulled Oracle Higher. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©@yhelfman via Canva, @Yurich84 from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Oracle sold $20 billion of stock and bonds days after capping new capital-market funding at that amount through fiscal 2030.

Bloomberg reported that Microsoft is winding down a 2023 deal to rent AI computing from Oracle on older Nvidia chips.

Cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% last quarter, but free cash flow was negative $5 billion as data center spending ran ahead.

Oracle's fiscal second-quarter report, expected in December, must show cloud revenue growth of 65% to 71% to match guidance.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) has crammed a quarter's worth of news into two weeks. On November 2, it priced $20 billion of new stock and bonds. Four days later, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) is winding down a deal to rent AI computing from Oracle.

Then the mood flipped. Strong results from CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) sparked a rally in AI cloud stocks on November 11, and Oracle rose with the group. It is also preparing to offer chips from Alphabet (GOOGL:NASDAQ) in its cloud starting in 2027.

Before that bounce, Oracle sat among AI cloud names down 32% to 48% this year. The open question is whether its funding plan and $664 billion backlog hold up as big buyers rethink their AI capacity.

Funding capped, then fully tapped

Oracle set this up at its October 28 investor day. It capped new capital-market funding through fiscal 2030 at $20 billion, excluding refinancing.

Five days later, it used the whole cap in one go:

86.2 million new shares at $116 each, for about $9.9 billion in net proceeds

$10 billion of senior notes

Both deals closed on November 4

That clears a funding overhang. However, it also adds dilution and fresh interest costs to a balance sheet already carrying heavy debt…

Oracle (ORCL): total debt, quarterly, $ billions, Q1 FY2025–Q1 FY2027 (TIKR)

Then came Microsoft. According to Bloomberg, the company has been switching off rented Oracle capacity since it declined to renew. The 2023 deal ran AI features in Bing on an older generation of Nvidia chips.

Oracle answered fast, and a spokesperson told Reuters that demand for its AI infrastructure "remains strong, including for earlier-generation GPUs."

The backlog still carries the case

Oracle never disclosed the Microsoft deal's terms. Yet its newer signings tell a fuller story. In the fiscal first quarter ended August 31, it booked more than $30 billion of new AI cloud contracts. Remaining performance obligations reached $664 billion, up $209 billion from a year earlier.
